query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloys, the simultaneous action of wear and corrosion at elevated temperature preferentially disrupts the protective oxide or passivating layers along the phase boundaries. This exposes the more corrosion-susceptible interphase regions to an aggressive environment, thereby accelerating both the mechanical and chemical degradation processes via a synergistic tribo-corrosion mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a well-defined interpenetrating microstructure produced by rapid solidification or directional solidification, resulting in alternating phases with distinct corrosion resistances.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloy to a combined loading regime where a sliding wear action (as in a pin-on-disk or reciprocating wear test) is applied concurrently with exposure to a corrosive medium (such as a saline environment) at an elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Testing conducted at an elevated temperature (e.g., 400–500 °C) in an aqueous 3.5% NaCl or similar corrosive electrolyte, with a controlled wear load and sliding velocity for a fixed duration. Parallel tests include isolated wear-only and corrosion-only conditions to serve as baselines.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between the different eutectic phases, which act as localized sites of stress concentration and accelerated breakdown of protective surface films.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically removes protective oxide/passive films preferentially at the phase boundaries, thereby exposing fresh, reactive surfaces. This exposure promotes localized corrosion through micro-galvanic coupling between phases. The elevated temperature accelerates oxidation kinetics, further weakening interphase interfaces such that the combined effect is greater than the sum of individual wear and corrosion effects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (exposure to wear-only or corrosion-only), the total degradation (as measured by mass loss and surface damage) will be higher under simultaneous wear-corrosion conditions. Additionally, both the wear scar depth/area and the density/size of corrosion pits will be amplified compared to the baseline cases.
generation.baseline: Degradation measured under identical elevated temperature conditions but with either only wear (non-corrosive atmosphere) or only corrosion (no mechanical loading), ensuring that the only difference is the absence of the coupled effect.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for eutectic high-entropy alloys with distinct phase separations, at temperatures where both wear-induced passive film removal and thermally accelerated corrosion kinetics are significant. It assumes that the corrosive medium and wear parameters are well controlled and that the scale of the alloy’s microstructural heterogeneity is on the order that makes phase boundary effects relevant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of wear and corrosion to the overall degradation, as well as the extent to which the microstructural details (e.g., phase size and distribution) amplify the coupling effect, are uncertain. Variations in alloy composition or testing parameters may lead to deviations from the predicted synergistic behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of samples from the same multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy. One set is exposed to wear-only in an inert atmosphere, the second to corrosion-only (no mechanical wear), and the third to simultaneous wear and corrosion under identical temperature and duration conditions. Use identical mechanical loading (e.g., pin-on-disk wear setup) and identical corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5% NaCl solution at 450 °C).
measurements: Mass loss and wear scar analysis (depth, width, and area) via profilometry and microscopy.
Corrosion pit density and depth using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX).
Surface chemical composition and oxide film integrity by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear-corrosion tests do not show a statistically significant increase (beyond the additive effects) in overall material degradation, wear scar dimensions, or corrosion pit metrics compared to the arithmetic sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only effects, then the hypothesis that the synergistic removal of protective films at phase boundaries drives accelerated degradation would be falsified.
